title: Auto-Dreamer: Learning Offline Memory Consolidation for Language Agents
claim: A memory system is defined by a typed entry store plus read and write operators, with consolidation as a learned write step.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, lettered A-C, with arrows in B and C
description: Three side-by-side light-blue rounded panels, each with a lettered title. Panel A, "Memory bank", shows a row of colored entries e1…em, with blue for semantic and yellow for procedural. Below it are the entry's fields: name (green), body (orange) and provenance links (orange). At the bottom is a source trajectory made of x, o and a tokens. Panel B, "Read operation", starts with a robot icon and a query box. The query goes down through a frozen sentence encoder to a similarity-ranked list of entries with scores 0.92, 0.87, 0.54 … 0.12. A dashed box marks the top-K, and K entries are output. Panel C, "Write operation", takes a working region of the bank. It fetches the provenance-linked trajectories, then a brain icon marks the consolidator, which has tool chips (search_memory, check_memory, get_source_trace, synthesize). The result is a compact replacement set that forms the post-consolidation bank. Arrows run top to bottom within panels B and C.
caption: Memory primitives and operations. (A) The memory bank B holds typed entries (semantic or procedural); each entry has a short name ni, a body si, and provenance links to source trajectories in the trajectory log T . (B) The read operator retrieves the top-K entries by cosine similarity between a frozen sentence encoder ϕ applied to the query and to each entry’s name-body text. (C) The write operator applies a learnable consolidator Cθ to a working region R ⊆B and its provenance-linked trajectories TR, producing a replacement set S that supersedes R in the post-consolidation bank B⋆.
abstract: Language agents increasingly operate over streams of related tasks, yet existing memory systems struggle to convert accumulated experience into reusable knowledge. Retrieval-augmented and structured memory methods record per-session observations effectively, but often couple acquisition and consolidation into a single online process, leaving the agent without a global view across sessions to discover recurring patterns, abstract shared procedures, or prune redundant entries. Inspired by complementary learning systems theory, we propose Auto-Dreamer, a learned offline consolidator for language-agent memory. Auto-Dreamer decouples fast per-session memory acquisition from slow cross-session consolidation. Given a selected working region of a typed memory bank, the consolidator treats the region as read-only evidence, performs bounded tool-use to inspect entries and provenance-linked source trajectories, and synthesizes a fresh compact replacement set that abstracts across sessions and supersedes the original region. We train Auto-Dreamer via GRPO, using end-to-end agent performance as the reward signal to learn how to consolidate memories acquired through fast online experience. Trained on ScienceWorld trajectories alone, Auto-Dreamer outperforms fixed, RL-trained, and prompted memory baselines on ScienceWorld by 7 points while using an active memory bank 12$\times$ smaller than the strongest baseline, and continues to lead on held-out ALFWorld and WebArena without retraining -- using 6$\times$ less memory than the strongest baseline on ALFWorld.
